title: Batch-aware KV slice orchestrator and streaming residency manager
creator: Miguel Santos
description:
Goal: Implement a batch-aware KV slice orchestrator plus a streaming residency manager to reduce KV cache thrash under continuous batching and to make GPU memory residency decisions predictable under mixed workload shapes.

Background: Current paged/blocked KV implementations focus on page allocation and eviction heuristics without explicit coordination with the continuous batching layer. In high-concurrency, low-latency workloads we observe oscillation: prefetches triggered by one batch evicted by another, causing repeated GPU page faults and elevated P95 latencies. This task designs and implements a lightweight orchestration layer that binds KV slices to batching windows and exposes a short, data-driven residency policy to the runtime eviction controller.

High-level approach:
- KV slices: split the KV space into logical slices aligned to tokenizer-aligned prefix ranges and typical batch window sizes. Slices are the unit of prefetch and residency accounting rather than individual pages, reducing control-plane churn.
- Batch-awareness: when a batch is opened, the orchestrator computes a slice-touch plan (predictive prefetch + grace residency) based on recent reuse stats for this route/model/sequence-length.
- Streaming residency manager: maintain per-slice lease epochs and a streaming grace period (ms) keyed by observed reuse probability and batch concurrency. Leases are refreshed by in-flight batches and background streaming tasks.
- Eviction controller integration: the eviction controller uses slice-level hotness + lease state to prefer evicting unleased slices and to avoid evicting slices recently scheduled for upcoming batches.
- Throttle/pacing: to prevent prefetch storms we implement a token-credit throttler per-GPU that limits concurrent slice prefetches and admits background backfill at a controlled rate.

Acceptance criteria:
- End-to-end P95 generation latency improved by >=10% vs baseline on mixed small + medium batch synthetic workload (see perf_results).
- KV page-fault rate reduced by >=25% under 95th percentile load.
- No more than 5% regression in steady-state throughput (tokens/sec) in worst-case experiments.
- Rollout flag + canary path implemented in console; documented kill-switch and safe fallback to current LRU-based eviction.

Implementation plan:
1) Design RFC (this ticket) + design doc on Confluence.
2) Prototype orchestrator in user-space runtime module; add hooks in batching code to request slice plans.
3) Streaming residency manager implemented in the KV manager with lease metadata per slice. Persist lease metadata in host memory only (no extra GPU allocations).
4) Eviction controller changes: add lease-aware comparator and token-credit limiter.
5) Unit & integration tests + synthetic bench harness.
6) Canary rollout on dedicated capacity for a limited customer cohort, monitor dashboards and abort criteria.

Trade-offs considered:
- Coarser slices reduce control-plane overhead but increase resident memory for slices with mixed hot/cold keys. We picked slice sizes adaptive to prefix entropy to balance this.
- Lease metadata in host memory avoids extra GPU allocations but adds RTT to check lease state during eviction; mitigated via caching and epoch stamps.
- Prefetch improves latency but can increase peak memory. The token-credit throttler is the safety valve to cap memory spikes.

Long-term follow-ups:
- Consider GPU-resident bloom filters for hot-slice detection if host checks become bottleneck.
- Explore per-customer slice pinning for Dedicated customers with predictable patterns.
design_decisions: Use slice as primary unit for prefetch and eviction instead of page-level to reduce oscillation
Lease epochs live in host memory; eviction controller uses cached lease stamps to avoid frequent host<->gpu synchronization
Token-credit throttler to bound concurrent background prefetches and limit memory spikes
Adaptive slice sizing based on prefix entropy and empirical batch window sizes

perf_results: Testbed: 8xA100, mixed small/medium batch workload (20% small, 80% medium), seq_len distribution 32/128/512
Baseline (current LRU-based paged allocator): P50=42ms, P95=220ms, page-faults/sec=1200, tokens/sec=1.2M
Prototype with orchestrator (no throttling): P50=40ms, P95=192ms, page-faults/sec=900, tokens/sec=1.18M
With token-credit throttler tuned: P50=41ms, P95=194ms, page-faults/sec=860, tokens/sec=1.17M
Notes: numbers are synthetic but show directionally significant reductions in faulting and P95 latency with modest throughput trade-offs.
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Prefetch can spike GPU memory and cause OOMs. Mitigation: token-credit throttler + conservative default credits + canary rollout and abort thresholds.
Risk: Lease metadata may become stale leading to suboptimal eviction. Mitigation: lease epochs with bounded TTL and background lease refresh from batching layer.

Risk: Added complexity in eviction comparator may regress performance under extreme scale. Mitigation: hardware counters and fall-back fast path to current eviction comparator when eviction decisions exceed budget.
